extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of ancient Greek philosophy (Plato's dialogues); general readers interested in ethics, rhetoric, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / analysis of an excerpt from Plato's Gorgias (philosophical dialogue debating justice, rhetoric, punishment, and the good life). Focuses on normative claims about punishment, rhetoric, natural vs. conventional justice, and the proper place of philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment as suffering administered by an agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Being punished is suffering and suffering implies an agent; he who punishes rightly, punishes justly, and he who is punished and suffers retribution, suffers justly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates leads through linked admissions: punishment is suffering → implies a punisher → a rightful punisher acts justly → therefore the punished suffer justly. This sets up subsequent moral inferences about punishment's role and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment benefits the soul (justice as medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: If he be justly punished his soul is improved; justice punishes us and makes us more just, and is the medicine of our vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates analogizes arts: money-making frees from poverty, medicine frees from disease, and justice frees from intemperance and injustice. Punishment is useful like medical treatment: painful but leading to the soul's health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice is the greatest evil of all
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice and all evil in the soul have been admitted to be the most disgraceful and, by extension, the greatest of evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues that among evils of estate, body, and soul, the soul's corruptions (injustice, ignorance, cowardice) are worst because they are most disgraceful and hurtful; this hierarchy grounds moral priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doing wrong and not being punished is the worst condition
rubrics_metrics.description: To do wrong and not to be punished is first and greatest of all evils; the doer of injustice who escapes punishment is more miserable than the sufferer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From premises about punishment improving the soul, Socrates concludes that escaping correction perpetuates vice and therefore produces the deepest misery—this reverses common praise of unpunished power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper moral use of rhetoric: confessing and exposing wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric may be useful to accuse oneself and one’s relations, to bring iniquity to light and not conceal it, so that the wrong-doer may suffer and be made whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates suggests rhetoric should be directed toward moral improvement—using persuasive skill to expose injustice (even one’s own) so justice can correct and heal the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper use of rhetoric: protecting or enabling injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is useful to those who wish to prevent punishment and to protect wrongdoers—e.g., preventing an enemy from being punished or enabling thieves/killers to escape consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates acknowledges this pragmatic use but distinguishes usefulness for the unjust from moral legitimacy: rhetoric can serve immoral ends (to keep the wicked unpunished) though that use harms the soul of its beneficiary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural justice versus conventional justice (superior vs. many)
rubrics_metrics.description: Callicles' doctrine: conventionally held justice (equality, condemning dishonesty) is a product of the weak; nature's justice is that the superior (stronger/wiser/braver) should rule over and have more than the inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callicles argues laws of the many serve weak interests; by contrast 'natural' law makes might right and legitimates the better taking more. This presents a counter-rubric for evaluating justice as power-based rather than equality-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: The strong should indulge and satisfy their desires (temperance denounced)
rubrics_metrics.description: True living for the strong consists in allowing desires to grow to the uttermost and having courage and intelligence to satisfy them; luxury and intemperance (when backed by means) are virtue and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callicles frames temperance as a restraint praised by the weak; evaluative standard here measures virtue by power and the ability to fulfill desires rather than by self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scope of philosophy in life (moderation in study)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy, if pursued in moderation and at the proper age, is an elegant accomplishment, but too much philosophy in later life makes a man ignorant of public affairs and ruinous to practical action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callicles criticizes excessive lifelong philosophical study as producing men who cannot speak or act effectively in courts or politics; the criterion is balance between theoretical study and practical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities for testing the good/evil of the soul: knowledge, good-will, outspokenness
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a complete trial of the good or evil of the soul one ought to have three qualities—knowledge, good-will, outspokenness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates treats agreement with a friend possessing these qualities as a 'touchstone' for truth: if such a person concurs, the tested point need not be further examined. This offers a methodological criterion for epistemic trust in interlocutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness: never having had vice is best; being cured is second
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness surely does not consist in being delivered from evils, but in never having had them; the happiest is he who never had vice, the second happiest is he delivered from vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the medical analogy, Socrates ranks states: lifelong moral purity beats recovery after corruption; this supplies a normative metric for evaluating moral states across people's lives.
